questions.rationale: Pain control makes deep breathing and walking possible, splinting reduces pain with coughing, and sitting up and walking expand the lungs. Oxygen is applied as prescribed. Lying flat worsens atelectasis, and fluids help keep secretions thin.

Show the client how to splint the incision with a pillow when coughing
Help the client sit up in a chair and walk as prescribed
Apply oxygen to keep the SpO2 at 92% or higher
Keep the client flat in bed until the fever goes away
Limit fluids to reduce secretions

questions.answer_summary: C

Evaluating the client's breath sounds after the walk
Helping the client walk in the hallway after the pain medicine takes effect

questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow-up.
questions.rationale: A painful vesicular rash in a band on one side of the body suggests shingles, and uncrusted lesions can spread varicella-zoster virus to people who are not immune, such as an immunocompromised roommate or a pregnant staff member without immunity. The temperature and respiratory rate are not concerns.

passage_segments.text: Fluid-filled blisters in a band on the right chest
Pregnant staff member who has never had chickenpox

questions.stem: For each staff member, indicate whether the LPN/VN should assign the staff member to care for this resident while the lesions are uncrusted.
questions.rationale: Staff with evidence of immunity, such as past chickenpox or two vaccine doses, can care for a resident with shingles. Staff without known immunity, especially those who are pregnant, should not be assigned because varicella can cause serious illness for them and harm a fetus.

rows.text: An RN who had chickenpox as a child
An assistive personnel who received two doses of varicella vaccine
A pregnant assistive personnel who has never had chickenpox
A float staff member whose immunity is unknown
An LPN/VN with documented immunity

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: Shingles is caused by reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus that stays dormant in nerve roots after chickenpox. It causes pain and then a vesicular rash in one dermatome that does not cross the midline. Contact dermatitis and cellulitis do not follow a dermatome.
questions.template: The resident most likely has ___1___, caused by ___2___.
questions.answer_summary: 1: herpes zoster (shingles); 2: reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus

questions.stem: The resident is not immunocompromised, and the rash is localized. Which infection control measures should the LPN/VN put in place? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: For localized shingles in a person who is not immunocompromised, standard precautions with the lesions completely covered until they crust are used, along with hand hygiene and separating the resident from people at high risk. Gloves do not protect a nonimmune pregnant staff member, and precautions are based on the lesions crusting, not on pain. Disseminated shingles or shingles in an immunocompromised person requires airborne and contact precautions.

options.text: Keep the lesions covered until they crust
Separate the resident from the roommate who is receiving chemotherapy
Perform hand hygiene after any contact with the lesions or dressings
Keep staff without immunity from caring for the resident
Allow the pregnant staff member to give care while wearing gloves
Stop precautions as soon as the pain improves

questions.answer_summary: A, B, C, D

questions.stem: The provider prescribes valacyclovir. Which statement by the LPN/VN about the medication is accurate?
questions.rationale: Antivirals such as valacyclovir shorten the illness and reduce pain when started within 72 hours of the rash and are taken for the full prescribed course. They do not eliminate the virus, and lesions must still be covered until crusted.
questions.answer_summary: B

options.text: "It will cure the virus completely so that shingles can never come back again."
"It works best when started within 72 hours of the rash."
"You only need to take it on days when the pain is very severe."
"It prevents the spread of shingles, so you no longer need to cover the rash."

questions.stem: On day 8, the charge nurse reviews how the case was managed. For each finding, indicate whether it shows effective management or needs follow-up.
questions.rationale: Protecting the roommate, appropriate staff assignments, crusted lesions, and controlled pain show effective management, and interest in the shingles vaccine supports prevention. A float staff member of unknown immunity caring for the resident is an exposure that must be reported and followed up through employee health.

rows.text: The roommate was moved to another room and has no rash
Only staff with immunity were assigned to the resident
The lesions are crusted, and pain is 3/10 with prescribed medication
A float staff member with unknown immunity cared for the resident overnight
The resident asks about the shingles vaccine after recovery

questions.rationale: The high bilirubin level indicates hyperbilirubinemia. Low intake in the first days means fewer stools, so more bilirubin is reabsorbed from the intestine; ABO incompatibility may also add to red cell breakdown. Frequent feeding helps, and sunlight is not a treatment.

questions.stem: The newborn is admitted for phototherapy. Which care measures should the LPN/VN include? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Eye shields protect the retinas, maximum skin exposure increases effectiveness, frequent feedings help remove bilirubin in stools, and temperature and output are monitored because phototherapy can cause overheating and fluid loss. Lotions can cause burns under the lights, and eye shields are removed during feedings outside the lights to support bonding.

options.text: Cover the eyes with protective shields while under the lights
Leave the newborn undressed except for a diaper
Breastfeed at least 8 to 12 times in 24 hours
Monitor temperature, wet diapers, and stools
Apply lotion to protect the skin from the lights
Keep the eye shields on during feedings out of the lights

questions.rationale: A lactation consultant can assess latch, milk transfer, and supply and help the parent breastfeed more effectively, which addresses the cause of the low intake. A dietitian, social worker, or physical therapist does not address breastfeeding technique.

options.text: A dietitian
A social worker
A physical therapist
A lactation consultant

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: Massive proteinuria, low albumin, high cholesterol, and generalized edema with a normal blood pressure are typical of nephrotic syndrome in young children. Loss of immune proteins in the urine and treatment with corticosteroids increase the risk of infection. Glomerulonephritis typically causes hypertension and dark, tea-colored urine with less edema.

questions.answer_summary: 1: nephrotic syndrome; 2: infection

questions.stem: Which instructions about prednisone should the LPN/VN reinforce with the parents? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Taking prednisone with food reduces stomach upset, infection precautions are important because of immunosuppression, and stopping suddenly can cause adrenal insufficiency, so the dose is tapered as prescribed. Increased appetite and mood changes are expected. Live vaccines are delayed during high-dose steroid therapy.

options.text: Give prednisone with food
Keep the child away from people with infections and report a fever
Do not stop prednisone suddenly
Expect increased appetite and mood changes
Schedule live vaccines during treatment
Stop prednisone as soon as the swelling goes away

questions.answer_summary: A, B, C, D

questions.stem: The child refuses to play and says, "I look like a balloon." What is the LPN/VN's best response?
questions.rationale: A simple, honest explanation that the swelling will improve with treatment, along with an activity that fits the child's energy level, supports a preschooler's coping. Denying the child's feelings, making a false promise, and avoiding the topic do not help.
questions.answer_summary: A

options.text: "The medicine will help the puffiness go away. Let's pick a game you can play in bed."
"You don't look like a balloon at all, so there is really nothing for you to be upset about."
"If you eat less salt, you'll look normal again by tomorrow morning when you wake up from your sleep."
"Let's not talk about how you look."

questions.rationale: Home urine testing, knowing when to report infection, and scheduled follow-up support a safe transition home. A plan to stop prednisone abruptly needs more teaching, and a cost barrier needs a social work referral through the RN before discharge.

Parent plans to stop prednisone when the swelling goes away

questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow-up.
questions.rationale: Coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, and vomiting with a lithium level of 2.2 mEq/L indicate toxicity. Dehydration, reduced kidney function, and ibuprofen, which decreases lithium excretion, explain the rise. A stable mood without self-harm thoughts is not a concern today.

passage_segments.text: Mood stable, with no thoughts of self-harm

questions.correct_text: Coarse hand tremor; Unsteady gait and slurred speech; Vomited twice this morning; Drinking less because of nausea; Lithium level 2.2 mEq/L; Creatinine 1.5 mg/dL; Ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily
questions.answer_summary: Coarse hand tremor; Unsteady gait and slurred speech; Vomited twice this morning; Drinking less because of nausea; Lithium level 2.2 mEq/L; Creatinine 1.5 mg/dL; Ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is an expected effect at a therapeutic lithium level or a sign of toxicity.
questions.rationale: A fine tremor, mild thirst, increased urination, and mild nausea early in therapy are common at therapeutic levels. A coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, and persistent vomiting and diarrhea are signs of toxicity that need immediate attention.

rows.text: Fine hand tremor
Mild thirst and increased urination
Coarse hand tremor
Unsteady gait and slurred speech
Persistent vomiting and diarrhea
Mild nausea when therapy is first started

questions.answer_summary: Fine hand tremor: Expected at a therapeutic level; Mild thirst and increased urination: Expected at a therapeutic level; Coarse hand tremor: Sign of toxicity; Unsteady gait and slurred speech: Sign of toxicity; Persistent vomiting and diarrhea: Sign of toxicity; Mild nausea when therapy is first started: Expected at a therapeutic level

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: Lithium is cleared by the kidneys. Fluid and sodium loss from vomiting and diarrhea and NSAIDs such as ibuprofen reduce its excretion, so the level rises to a toxic range. High sodium intake and missed doses would lower the level.
questions.template: The client is most likely experiencing ___1___, caused by ___2___.

options: dehydration and ibuprofen reducing lithium excretion
too much sodium in the diet
blanks.correct: dehydration and ibuprofen reducing lithium excretion

questions.answer_summary: 1: lithium toxicity; 2: dehydration and ibuprofen reducing lithium excretion

questions.stem: Which actions should the LPN/VN take? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: With signs of toxicity and a high level, the next dose is held and the provider is notified immediately, usually leading to emergency evaluation. The client's unsteadiness requires supervision, and the provider needs to know about the NSAID. Salt loading is not done independently, and sending the client home is unsafe.

options.text: Hold the next lithium dose
Notify the RN and provider of the lithium level and symptoms right away
Stay with the client because of the risk of falling
Report the client's ibuprofen use to the provider
Encourage the client to take the next dose with extra salt
Send the client home to rest and recheck the level next week

questions.answer_summary: A, B, C, D

questions.stem: Which instruction should the LPN/VN reinforce to help prevent another episode?
questions.rationale: Adequate fluids and avoiding NSAIDs unless approved help keep lithium levels stable. Sharply reducing sodium raises lithium levels, missed or skipped doses should be discussed with the provider, and stopping lithium can cause relapse.
questions.answer_summary: A

options.text: Drink about 2 to 3 L of fluid daily and check with the provider before taking NSAIDs
Cut back on salt as much as possible to keep the lithium level from rising again
Skip lithium doses on days when you feel nauseated
Stop lithium once your mood has been stable for a month

questions.stem: At a follow-up visit after recovery, the LPN/VN reviews the client's progress. For each finding, indicate whether it shows progress or needs follow-up.
questions.rationale: Stable mood and sleep, regular therapy, recognizing early warning signs, and a crisis plan show good self-management. Thinking about stopping lithium after the toxicity episode raises the risk of relapse, so the LPN/VN reports it so the provider can discuss the client's concerns and options.

rows.text: Mood stable, sleeping about 7 hours a night
Attends weekly therapy sessions
Names early warning signs of mania, such as needing less sleep
Has a written crisis plan
Says, "I'm thinking about stopping lithium because of what happened."

questions.answer_summary: Mood stable, sleeping about 7 hours a night: Progress; Attends weekly therapy sessions: Progress; Names early warning signs of mania, such as needing less sleep: Progress; Has a written crisis plan: Progress; Says, "I'm thinking about stopping lithium because of what happened.": Needs follow-up

case_studies.scenario: A 54-year-old client is on the second day after an open colectomy. The client smokes 1 pack of cigarettes a day and is reluctant to move because of pain.

exhibits.label: Nurses' notes, 0900

exhibits.label: Vital signs, 0900
exhibits.content: T 100.2°F (37.9°C), HR 98/min, RR 24/min and shallow, BP 132/78 mm Hg, SpO2 91% on room air.

exhibits.label: Prescriptions
exhibits.content: Oxycodone 5 mg by mouth every 4 hours as needed for pain. Incentive spirometer 10 times an hour while awake. Walk in the hallway 3 times a day. Oxygen by nasal cannula to keep SpO2 at 92% or higher.

case_studies.scenario: A 38-year-old client with bipolar I disorder who takes lithium comes to the outpatient mental health clinic. The client started ibuprofen for back pain 1 week ago and has had diarrhea for 2 days.

exhibits.label: Nurses' notes
exhibits.content: Coarse hand tremor. Unsteady gait and slurred speech. Vomited twice this morning. Five episodes of diarrhea in 24 hours. Says, "I feel foggy." Has been drinking less because of nausea. Mood stable, with no thoughts of self-harm.

exhibits.label: Laboratory results
exhibits.content: Lithium level 2.2 mEq/L (therapeutic 0.6–1.2). Sodium 133 mEq/L (135–145). Creatinine 1.5 mg/dL (0.6–1.2).

exhibits.label: Medications
exhibits.content: Lithium carbonate 300 mg by mouth three times daily. Ibuprofen 600 mg by mouth three times daily, over the counter.
